name: Deep Red
lede: Deep red is a descriptive color name, a dark and saturated red; no book we read ties it to one pigment, dye or place, but its alternate names in old color lists are mostly iron-oxide earths.

sections.title: A description, not a pigment
sections.body:
Deep red is a plain description: a red that is dark and saturated. Our library carries it from two sources, the ISCC-NBS color names of 1955 and the xkcd color survey of 2010, and the swatch on this page is `#9A0200` [1]. No book we read treats it as the name of a particular pigment, dye or place. What the books do show is how often writers reach for the words when they describe something red and dark [2][3][4].

The library lists many alternate names for this swatch, all from ISCC-NBS block 40, and they are mostly materials [1]. They include Iron Oxide Red, Iron Red, Spanish Brown, Scarlet Ochre, Persian Earth, Majolica Earth, Purple Ochre and Red Ox [1]. Maerz and Paul recorded Majolica Earth and Agate in 1598, Persian Earth in 1735 and Scarlet Ochre in 1764 [1]. The dark red that people name "deep" turns out, in the old color lists, to be mostly iron-oxide earth, the family of [[indian-red]] and [[venetian-red]] [1].

sections.title: Deep red in the dyer's vat
sections.body:
Dyers were first to need the words. Ball notes that among the finest ancient dyes was a deep red obtained from an insect, and ties it to Isaiah's line about sins that are like scarlet [3]. After cochineal reached Europe from the Americas, wealthy buyers demanded cloth in this new deep red, often called *grana* or "in grain", Finlay writes [5]. In present-day Oaxaca a dyer still ground cochineal and finished the bath with alum, acacia fruits and lime juice to darken and intensify the deep red, Greenfield reports [6].

Madder gives a deep red too. The Compendium reports that Gentele in 1860 found partial precipitation of madder dye with soda or potash gave a deep red lake, while complete precipitation gave a lighter one [7]. Coles adds brazilwood, a hardwood that gives a deep red dye and supplied the cool reds of medieval lake pigments (see [[brazil-red]]) [8]. Ball also notes that the old purple of the dyers ran from bluish to a deep red depending on preparation, which is a reminder that ancient color words were wide [3].

sections.title: Deep red from the ground
sections.body:
Mineral reds are the other source. St Clair describes the walls of the Villa of Mysteries at Pompeii as an intense ground of deep red vermilion [4]. Finlay's account of icon painters names a deep red from Spanish mercury, presumably cinnabar, the ore of [[vermilion]] [9]. Stones belong here too: Ball explains that chromium impurities make corundum deep red in ruby, and sea-green in emerald, because the crystal field around the chromium is stronger in emerald [3]. A look at [[gem:ruby|ruby]] shows the red.

Earths are the oldest case. Red iron oxide has stained objects deep red since the Upper Paleolithic, some 50,000 years ago [4]. The Compendium lists Armenian bole as a deep red ochre from Cappadocia, and Paterson gives *almagra* as a deep red ochre found in Spain [7][2].

sections.title: A crowd of other names
sections.body:
Paterson's dictionary uses "deep red" as a gloss for a long list of names. Castillian, Iraq red, oxheart, para-red and Parma red are all described as a deep red, and *grenat* is the deep red of the garnet, which Paterson notes is an anagram of the stone [2]. *Sang-de-boeuf*, "ox blood", is a deep red glaze on old Chinese porcelain [2]. The shared idea is a red that is dark enough to need a second word.

Clothes carry the words too. In Nella Larsen's novel *Quicksand*, the teacher Helga Crane is thought strange for wearing "deep reds" at a school where bright colors are considered vulgar, and she is expected to wear black, brown and navy [10]. The color was a mark of how a person was allowed to look.

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
In our archive of 23,781 paintings, this swatch is present in 178 (0.75 per cent), and in 171 by the stricter within-painting count [11]. That is more common than 68 per cent of the named colors [11]. Inside a painting it is an accent in 91 per cent of the 171 [11].

It peaks in the 1400s, in 28 of 945 paintings (3.0 per cent), 3.6 times the museums' baseline [11]. One hit is [[painting:commons-Q134545315|Botticelli's portrait of a young man with a red cap]] of 1484, in which a color within six units of the swatch covers about a third of the canvas [11]. The first dated painting that holds it is from 1391, by Niccolo di Pietro Gerini, a floor and not a first [11]. It shares canvases with Dark Sienna and Dark chocolate brown more often than chance, with a lift of 6.6 and 2.6 [11]. As ever these are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so a match is not a pigment test [11].

questions.q: What did dyers call the deep red cloth made with cochineal when it reached Europe?

openers: Old color lists file Iron Oxide Red, Spanish Brown and Scarlet Ochre under the same swatch as Deep Red.
Chromium makes the same crystal deep red in ruby and sea-green in emerald.

issues: Hedged Finlay's 'Spanish mercury' red as presumably cinnabar (the book does not name cinnabar).
